analysis.one_liner: Temporarily guarantees up to $100 million of FDIC insurance per bank account and eases rules for rescuing or selling big failed banks.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Banking Committee, which held a hearing but never voted on it, so it died at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: After several bank failures in early 2023 raised fears about large uninsured deposits, this bill would have temporarily raised FDIC insurance on business checking-type accounts from the standard $250,000 to $100 million per depositor. It also would have let the FDIC approve mergers or sales of very large failed banks even when that costs the deposit insurance fund more than a straight liquidation, and would have let bank holding companies buy struggling banks for 90 days without the usual regulatory or antitrust review. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held one hearing, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The clearest beneficiaries would be large corporate and institutional depositors — businesses, nonprofits, and wealthy account holders — whose operating balances far above $250,000 would be fully insured for two years. Large bank holding companies would also gain: a 90-day window to buy distressed banks without regulatory approval or antitrust review, and, if they run a bank of $100 billion or more that fails, an FDIC resolution process adjusted to count the wider damage of a big-bank liquidation, making rescue-by-merger easier. Reciprocal deposit networks, which let banks split large deposits across institutions to maximize insurance coverage, would see their limits doubled.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big banks and large corporate depositors

how_it_helps.text: For two years, the FDIC would insure up to $100 million per depositor in noninterest-bearing transaction accounts, far above the standard $250,000 limit, protecting businesses and wealthy depositors from losing operating cash in a bank failure.

In a failure of a bank with at least $100 billion in assets, the FDIC could arrange a merger, sale, or acquisition under a modified least-cost test that counts the ripple effects of a plain-vanilla liquidation, making it easier to rescue or sell a large failing bank.

For 90 days after enactment, regulators' approval would not be needed for a holding company to acquire a bank whose stock had fallen 20% since March 2023, and such deals would be exempt from antitrust premerger review.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary depositors would pay little directly, but the deposit insurance fund — financed by fees on all banks and ultimately passed to customers — would absorb extra costs under the relaxed resolution standard, and bank consolidation would proceed with less scrutiny. Businesses and households also benefit less than big depositors from the expanded guarantee.
analysis.who_pays_short: The FDIC insurance fund and bank customers

drawbacks.text: The 90-day fast track would have let bank holding companies buy failing banks with no regulatory approval and no Clayton Act antitrust review, reducing scrutiny of consolidation in an already concentrated industry.

The adjusted least-cost resolution provision would let the FDIC facilitate mergers or sales of large failed banks even when that costs the deposit insurance fund more under a normal accounting, shifting potential losses toward the fund that banks and their customers finance.

Extending near-unlimited FDIC insurance to noninterest-bearing transaction accounts mostly benefits large businesses and wealthy depositors rather than ordinary savers, whose accounts are already well under the $250,000 standard limit.

Critics of blanket large-deposit guarantees argue they encourage banks to take greater risks because big depositors have less reason to monitor them — a moral-hazard cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated benefit is stability: guaranteeing large operating accounts and giving the FDIC more room to arrange sales could reduce the odds of contagious bank runs like the ones in spring 2023. But the costs fall on the structures that keep banks disciplined — antitrust and regulatory review of mergers and a resolution standard designed to spare the fund from covering large banks' losses. If those standards are lowered only when a big bank fails, the largest institutions get a separate, easier rule, and depositors and small banks ultimately fund the difference through FDIC assessments. The bill also never advanced far enough for these trade-offs to be tested in a floor debate.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee held one hearing on it but never voted, and the full Senate never considered it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Hagerty introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
On June 22, 2023, the Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill (printed as S.Hrg. 118-453) — the only committee activity beyond the referral.
The bill attracted no cosponsors and was never reported out of committee, voted on, or taken up by the House before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The cosponsor list stayed at zero for the life of the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The regulatory status quo — FDIC's standard $250,000 limit, its strict least-cost resolution duty, and normal merger and antitrust review of bank acquisitions — all survived intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The regulatory status quo; no side won

for.name: Sen. Bill Hagerty
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Depositor Protection Act of 2023 and was its only sponsor.

for.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and held one hearing on June 22, 2023, but took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a cosponsor from either party and never reached a vote, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill would give big banks a softer resolution path when they fail, easier acquisition of distressed rivals without antitrust review, and insured large deposits that make funding cheaper. Nothing in the bill imposes a comparable benefit on ordinary savers.

Smaller banks (under $250 billion in assets) could opt out of the expanded insurance and avoid related fees, and they could not use the distressed-bank fast track themselves, but the easier acquisition rules would make them potential takeover targets.

Payroll and operating accounts far above $250,000 would be fully insured for two years, removing the risk that a bank failure wipes out a company's cash — a protection ordinary households never needed because their deposits are already under the limit.

industries.industry: FDIC and the deposit insurance fund
industries.note: The FDIC would gain new tools to handle large failures, but the modified least-cost test would let it spend more than a strict accounting would allow, placing potential losses on the insurance fund financed by banks and, ultimately, their customers.
